claim: Green leaf volatiles (GLVs) constitute a widespread group of defensive plant volatiles that convey a herbivory-specific message via their isomeric composition.
source: Green leaf volatiles (GLVs) constitute a widespread group of defensive plant volatiles that convey a herbivory-specific message via their isomeric composition
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including volatile collection data showing isomeric shifts and behavioral assays.

claim: Feeding of the tobacco hornworm Manduca sexta converts (Z)-3- to (E)-2-GLVs thereby attracting predatory insects.
source: feeding of the tobacco hornworm Manduca sexta converts (Z)-3- to (E)-2-GLVs thereby attracting predatory insects
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to previous work (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: The isomeric shift in GLVs was detected in the host plant Datura wrightii.
source: We detected the isomeric shift in the host plant Datura wrightii
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Tables 1-2.

claim: Two isomer-specific regions responding to either (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenyl acetate were identified in the antennal lobe of M. sexta females.
source: We identified two isomer-specific regions responding to either (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenyl acetate
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by functional imaging data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Ovipositing Manduca moths preferred (Z)-3-perfumed D. wrightii over (E)-2-perfumed plants in field experiments.
source: Field experiments demonstrated that ovipositing Manduca moths preferred (Z)-3-perfumed D. wrightii over (E)-2-perfumed plants
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by field oviposition assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: (E)-2-GLVs and/or specific (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios provide information regarding host plant attack by conspecifics that ovipositing hawkmoths use for host plant selection.
source: These results show that (E)-2-GLVs and/or specific (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios provide information regarding host plant attack by conspecifics that ovipositing hawkmoths use for host plant selection
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of volatile analysis, neurophysiology, and behavioral experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon herbivory, plants respond with an increased release and de novo synthesis of several volatile compounds from their vegetative tissues.
source: Upon herbivory, plants respond with an increased release and de novo synthesis of several volatile compounds from their vegetative tissues (Mumm and Dicke, 2010)
evidence: This is a general statement about plant responses to herbivory supported by citation to Mumm and Dicke, 2010.

claim: Herbivore induced plant volatiles can provide significant information to the surrounding environment as composition and abundance reflect several biotic and abiotic factors.
source: These so-called herbivore induced plant volatiles can provide significant information to the surrounding environment as composition and abundance reflect several biotic and abiotic factors (Takabayashi et al., 1995; De Moraes et al., 1998; Gouinguené et al., 2001; Schuman et al., 2009; Hare, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The antennal lobe (AL) of M. sexta females consists of about 70 structural and functional subunits called olfactory glomeruli.
source: The AL of M. sexta females consists of about 70 structural and functional subunits called olfactory glomeruli (Grosse-Wilde et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a factual statement about M. sexta anatomy supported by citation to Grosse-Wilde et al., 2011.

claim: OSNs expressing the same receptor, and thus responding to the same set of odorants, converge onto the same glomerulus in the AL.
source: OSNs expressing the same receptor, and thus responding to the same set of odorants, converge onto the same glomerulus in the AL (Gao et al., 2000; Vosshall, 2000) as has been demonstrated for Drosophila melanogaster and indirectly also in several moth species (Hansson, 1997)
evidence: This is a general principle of olfactory system organization supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Green leaf volatiles are characterized by a C6-backbone.
source: Green leaf volatiles (GLVs) constitute a large group of herbivore-induced plant volatiles characterized by a C6-backbone
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the chemical structure of GLVs.

claim: GLVs are emitted only in trace amounts from healthy, undamaged plant tissue, but are emitted instantly after cell disruption.
source: While emitted only in trace amounts from healthy, undamaged plant tissue, they are emitted instantly after cell disruption (Turlings et al., 1995; D'Auria et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim about GLV emission patterns is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GLVs are generated from C18-fatty acids via the enzymes lipoxygenase (LOX) and hydroperoxide lyase (HPL).
source: GLVs are generated from C18-fatty acids via the enzymes lipoxygenase (LOX) and hydroperoxide lyase (HPL; Allmann et al., 2010)
evidence: This describes the biosynthetic pathway of GLVs and is supported by citation.

claim: (Z)-3-hexenal originates from the cleavage of α-linolenic acid through the activity of HPL and it partly rearranges to (E)-2-hexenal.
source: One of the most abundant GLVs, (Z)-3-hexenal, originates from the cleavage of α-linolenic acid through the activity of HPL and it partly rearranges to (E)-2-hexenal
evidence: This describes the specific biosynthetic pathway and isomerization of hexenal.

claim: Both alkenals can be further metabolized by an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and alcohol acyltransferase (AAT) to the corresponding alcohols and their esters.
source: Both alkenals can be further metabolized by an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and alcohol acyltransferase (AAT; D'Auria et al., 2007) to the corresponding alcohols and their esters (Matsui, 2006)
evidence: This describes the enzymatic conversion of GLV aldehydes to alcohols and esters, supported by citations.

claim: GLVs have been assigned various plant defense-associated functions by directly inhibiting phytopathogens.
source: GLVs have been assigned various plant defense-associated functions by directly inhibiting phytopathogens (Hamilton-Kemp et al., 1992; Nakamura and Hatanaka, 2002; Prost et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim about GLV functions is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GLVs repel several herbivore species.
source: GLVs have been assigned various plant defense-associated functions by directly inhibiting phytopathogens (Hamilton-Kemp et al., 1992; Nakamura and Hatanaka, 2002; Prost et al., 2005) and repelling several herbivore species (De Moraes et al., 2001; Kessler and Baldwin, 2001; Vancanneyt et al., 2001; Zhang and Schlyter, 2004)
evidence: This claim about GLV functions is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GLVs function as indirect plant defenses by attracting foraging predators and host-seeking parasitoids to the plant and its attacker.
source: Remarkably, GLVs also function as indirect plant defenses by attracting foraging predators and host-seeking parasitoids to the plant and its attacker (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001; Shiojiri et al., 2006; Halitschke et al., 2008; Schuman et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim about GLV functions is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GLVs are thought to act as nonspecific signals of plant damage due to their ubiquity and instant release.
source: Due to their ubiquity and instant release, GLVs are thought to act as nonspecific signals of plant damage (Hatanaka et al., 1987; Hoballah et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim about the general perception of GLV function is supported by citations.

claim: An enzymatic component of the oral secretions (OS) of M. sexta larvae adds an herbivory-specific feature to the GLV signal.
source: We recently showed that an enzymatic component of the oral secretions (OS) of M. sexta larvae adds an herbivory-specific feature to the GLV signal
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, which is then described in detail.

claim: Mechanically damaged leaves of Nicotiana attenuata released large amounts of (Z)-3-GLVs and low amounts of (E)-2-GLVs.
source: Mechanically damaged leaves of Nicotiana attenuata released large amounts of (Z)-3-GLVs and low amounts of (E)-2-GLVs
evidence: This describes previous experimental results from the authors' earlier work.

claim: When N. attenuata was attacked by M. sexta caterpillars or when puncture wounds were treated with M. sexta's OS, the amount of (E)-2-GLVs released increased, while the amount of (Z)-3-GLVs decreased, resulting in a distinct change in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of GLV emissions.
source: However, when the plant was attacked by M. sexta caterpillars or when puncture wounds of plant leaves were treated with M. sexta's OS, the amount of (E)-2-GLVs released increased, while the amount of (Z)-3-GLVs decreased, resulting in a distinct change in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of GLV emissions
evidence: This describes previous experimental results from the authors' earlier work.

claim: The herbivore-induced change in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio attracted the generalist hemipteran predator Geocoris spp., which decreased the herbivore load on the plant by feeding on herbivore eggs.
source: This herbivore-induced change in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio attracted the generalist hemipteran predator Geocoris spp., which decreased the herbivore load on the plant by feeding on herbivore eggs (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010)
evidence: This describes previous experimental results from the authors' earlier work, supported by citation.

claim: A (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase was discovered in the OS of M. sexta larvae.
source: Our discovery of a (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase in the OS of M. sexta larvae raises many questions
evidence: This refers to a discovery from previous work by the authors.

claim: The specific isomerase activity occurs in at least two other lepidopteran species.
source: The occurrence of this specific isomerase activity in at least two other lepidopteran species (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010) however, suggests that it may have a beneficial function that outweighs the larva's net costs of maintaining such an enzyme
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reduced oviposition of Manduca moths in response to feeding damage has been shown in field experiments with M. quinquemaculata.
source: Reduced oviposition of Manduca moths in response to feeding damage has been shown in field experiments with M. quinquemaculata (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Reduced oviposition of Manduca moths in response to feeding damage has been shown under laboratory conditions with M. sexta.
source: Reduced oviposition of Manduca moths in response to feeding damage has been shown in field experiments with M. quinquemaculata (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001) as well as under laboratory conditions with M. sexta (Spaethe et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Datura is a highly preferred host plant of both M. sexta and the congeneric M. quinquemaculata for both nectar feeding and oviposition.
source: Datura is a highly preferred host plant of both M. sexta and the congeneric M. quinquemaculata for both nectar feeding (Alarcón et al., 2008; Kessler, 2012) and oviposition (Spaethe et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The distribution of Datura wrightii covers southwestern USA overlapping with the occurrence of both Manduca species.
source: Its distribution covers southwestern USA (Avery, 1959; Munz, 1973) overlapping with the occurrence of both Manduca species
evidence: This claim about geographic distribution is supported by citations.

claim: The perennial shrub D. wrightii is repeatedly described to quickly regrow leaves after herbivore damage.
source: The perennial shrub is repeatedly described to quickly regrow leaves after herbivore damage (Bronstein et al., 2009; Reisenman et al., 2010, 2013)
evidence: This claim about plant regrowth is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Laboratory experiments failed to find reduced oviposition on damaged D. wrightii.
source: Laboratory experiments failed to find reduced oviposition on damaged D. wrightii (Reisenman et al., 2013; Spaethe et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim about previous experimental results is supported by citations.

claim: D. wrightii responds to Manduca herbivore attack by emitting GLVs.
source: As the previously examined N. attenuata (Gaquerel et al., 2009), D. wrightii, respond to Manduca herbivore attack by emitting GLVs (Hare and Sun, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Manduca moths oviposit at twilight and night.
source: Manduca moths oviposit at twilight and night (Madden and Chamberlin, 1945; Lingren et al., 1977)
evidence: This claim about moth behavior is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In several plant species GLV emission has been shown to occur also in the dark period.
source: Therefore, we decided to collect volatiles during these times instead. We expected the shift to occur also during the night, as in several plant species GLV emission has been shown to occur also in the dark period (Loughrin et al., 1994; Arimura et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The shift in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio is caused by M. sexta oral secretions and not by the plant itself.
source: the respective shift in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio is caused by M. sexta oral secretions and not by the plant itself (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Volatile emissions vary with light regime.
source: However, volatile emissions vary with light regime (Halitschke et al., 2000; De Moraes et al., 2001; Gouinguene and Turlings, 2002; Morker and Roberts, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata has been shown to recognize and avoid altered ratios of (Z)-3- and (E)-2-GLVs emitted by its host plant Solanum tuberosum.
source: In classical host recognition experiments the Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata has been shown to recognize and avoid altered ratios of (Z)-3- and (E)-2-GLVs emitted by its host plant Solanum tuberosum (Visser and Avé, 1978)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Enantioselectivity has been reported for projection neurons in the female AL of M. sexta in response to (+)- and (−)-linalool.
source: Furthermore, enantioselectivity has been reported for projection neurons in the female AL of M. sexta in response to (+)- and (−)-linalool (Reisenman et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Application of M. sexta OS to leaf wounds of Datura wrightii causes a significant decrease in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of the GLVs released during the day compared with control plants.
source: During the day, application of OS onto wounds caused a significant decrease in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of the GLVs released from Datura plants compared with control plants (Figure 1A, day)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of the aldehydes differed significantly between treatments also at sunset and night light intensities.
source: The (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of the aldehydes differed significantly between treatments also at sunset and night light intensities (Figure 1A, sunset)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of w + w treated plants decreased with decreasing light intensities, which was mainly caused by increased (E)-2-hexenal emissions.
source: However, the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio of w + w treated plants also decreased with decreasing light intensities, which was mainly caused by increased (E)-2-hexenal emissions (Figure 3 and Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Treatment-dependent differences in (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios for the alcohol and the hexenyl acetate decreased under lower light conditions and were not found during the night.
source: Correspondingly, treatment-dependent differences in (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios for the alcohol and the hexenyl acetate decreased under lower light conditions and were not found during the night (Figure 1A, sunset, night)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During the day in field experiments, the application of OS to the wounds caused a significant increase in (E)-2-hexenal emissions compared with w+w treated leaves.
source: During the day the application of OS to the wounds caused a significant increase in (E)-2-hexenal emissions compared with w+w treated leaves (Figure 1B, day, and Table 2, day)
evidence: This claim is supported by field experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Table 2.

claim: (Z)-3-hexenal was not detectable in any of the field samples.
source: Similar to previous experiments with N. attenuata (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010) we were unable to detect (Z)-3-hexenal in any of the samples
evidence: This is a direct observation from the field experiments.

claim: During the first night field experiment, plants of both treatments released very high but similar amounts of (E)-2-hexenal, and the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios of the alcohols and hexenyl acetates were low, but did not differ between treatments.
source: During the first night-experiment (first night, average temperature 17.6 ± 0.7°C, wind speed 1.1 ± 0.8 m/s, waxing crescent lunar illumination with 9% of the moon illuminated), plants of both treatments released very high but similar amounts of (E)-2-hexenal, and the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios of the alcohols and hexenyl acetates were low, but did not differ between treatments, resembling the results of the night trapping in the growth chamber (Figure 1B, first night, and Table 2, first night)
evidence: This claim is supported by field experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Table 2.

claim: During the second night field experiment, w + OS-treated plants released significantly higher amounts of (E)-2-hexenal (twofold increase compared with w + w treated plants) and the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios of the hexenols and hexenyl acetates were significantly lower compared with mechanically wounded plants that were treated with water only.
source: During the second experiment (second night; average temperature 24.6 ± 0.8°C, wind speed 0.7 ± 0.8 m/s, full moon), approximately 2 weeks later, w + OS-treated plants released significantly higher amounts of (E)-2-hexenal (twofold increase compared with w + w treated plants) and the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios of the hexenols and hexenyl acetates were significantly lower compared with mechanically wounded plants that were treated with water only (Figure 1B, second night)
evidence: This claim is supported by field experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Odor-evoked calcium changes in response to exposure to the pure (E)-2- and (Z)-3-isomers of hexenal, hexenol and hexenyl acetate led to activity in discrete regions corresponding to specific glomeruli in the AL of M. sexta females.
source: Odor-evoked calcium changes in response to exposure to the pure (E)-2- and (Z)-3-isomers of hexenal, hexenol and hexenyl acetate led to activity in discrete regions corresponding to specific glomeruli in the AL of M. sexta females (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Aldehyde and alcohol structural isomers activated one single specific region (ROI 2), with significantly stronger responses to the (E)-2- compared with (Z)-3-isomers.
source: Aldehyde and alcohol structural isomers activated one single specific region (region of interest 2 [ROI 2], green), with significantly stronger responses to the (E)-2- compared with (Z)-3-isomers (Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate and its structural isomer activated three different regions in the female AL: a significantly (Z)-3-specific (ROI 3), a significantly (E)-2-specific (ROI 4) and an isomer-unspecific region (ROI 1).
source: (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate and its structural isomer activated three different regions in the female AL: a significantly (Z)-3-specific (ROI 3, blue), a significantly (E)-2-specific (ROI 4, pink) and an isomer-unspecific region (ROI 1, grey, Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The differences in activation patterns caused by stimulations with (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenyl acetate strongly suggest that the two odors activated OSNs expressing different sets of odorant receptor types on the female antennae.
source: The differences in activation patterns caused by stimulations with (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenyl acetate (Figure 4C) strongly suggest that the two odors activated OSNs expressing different sets of odorant receptor types on the female antennae
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In ROI 3, calcium signals evoked by (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate-containing mixtures were significantly higher compared with stimulations with pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate, which in turn did not differ from the mineral oil control.
source: In ROI 3 (blue) calcium signals evoked by (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate-containing mixtures were significantly higher compared with stimulations with pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate, which in turn did not differ from the mineral oil control (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For the (E)-2-specific ROI 4, stimulation with pure (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate led to significantly lower calcium responses when compared with pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate and the 20/80 ratio, but was not different from stimulation with mineral oil.
source: For the (E)-2-specific ROI 4 (pink) stimulation with pure (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate led to significantly lower calcium responses when compared with pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate and the 20/80 ratio, but was not different from stimulation with mineral oil (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Calcium responses of the unspecific ROI 1 did not differ between the structural isomers and their mixtures.
source: Calcium responses of the unspecific ROI 1 (in grey) did not differ between the structural isomers and their mixtures (Figure 5B)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stimulations with pure structural isomers as well as the 20% (Z)-3/80% (E)-2 mixture led to significantly different levels of neural activity in the (E)-2/(Z)-3-specific regions.
source: When comparing odor-evoked activation by different (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios in ROI 3 and 4, stimulations with pure structural isomers as well as the 20% (Z)-3/80% (E)-2 mixture led to significantly different levels of neural activity in these (E)-2/(Z)-3-specific regions (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Activation patterns differed significantly for pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate compared with the 50/50 and 80/20 (Z)-3/(E)-2 mixtures as well as for pure (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate compared with the 20/80 mixture.
source: Activation patterns differed significantly for pure (E)-2-hexenyl acetate compared with the 50/50 and 80/20 (Z)-3/(E)-2 mixtures as well as for pure (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate compared with the 20/80 mixture (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No differences were found between the isomeric mixtures (20/80; 50/50; 80/20).
source: However, no differences were found between the isomeric mixtures (20/80; 50/50; 80/20)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the functional imaging experiments.

claim: The level of activation of the (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate-specific ROI 3 was solely dependent on the presence of the (Z)-3-isomer and did not change with various amounts of it in the isomeric mixtures.
source: The level of activation of the (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate-specific ROI 3 (x-axis) was solely dependent on the presence of the (Z)-3-isomer and did not change with various amounts of it in the isomeric mixtures (ranging from 50 ng in 20/80 to 250 ng in 100/0)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The calcium signal in ROI 4 increased gradually with increasing percentage of the (E)-2-isomer up to 80% in the isomeric mixtures.
source: In contrast, the calcium signal in ROI 4 (y-axis) increased gradually with increasing percentage of the (E)-2-isomer up to 80% in the isomeric mixtures
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ROI 4 is able to convey information about the ratio of (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate in a mixture.
source: Thus, ROI 4 is able to convey information about the ratio of (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate in a mixture
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dose-dependent response characteristics of ROI 4.

claim: When plants were augmented with isomerically pure mixtures that consisted of either (Z)-3 or (E)-2-GLVs, Manduca moths laid significantly more eggs on the (Z)-3 than on the (E)-2-scented side of the plant.
source: When plants were augmented with isomerically pure mixtures that consisted of either (Z)-3 or (E)-2-GLVs (aldehyde, alcohol, hexenyl acetate and hexenyl butyrate, Table 3) Manduca moths laid significantly more eggs on the (Z)-3 than on the (E)-2-scented side of the plant (mean ± SEM number of eggs oviposited per plant side: (Z)-3-isomers 1.0 ± 0.2, (E)-2-isomers 0.5 ± 0.1, Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by field oviposition assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When comparing two GLV mixes that contained all tested (Z)-3 and (E)-2-GLVs in a balanced isomeric ratio (1:1) or in a high (Z)-3 vs (E)-2-ratio (9:1), significantly more eggs were oviposited on the sides of the plants that were scented with the higher (9:1) (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio.
source: When we compared two GLV mixes that contained all tested (Z)-3 and (E)-2-GLVs in a balanced isomeric ratio (1:1) or in a high (Z)-3 vs (E)-2-ratio (9:1), significantly more eggs were oviposited on the sides of the plants that were scented with the higher (9:1) (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio (9:1-ratio 1.8 ± 0.2; 1:1-ratio 0.6 ± 0.2; Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by field oviposition assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When comparing the two different hexenyl acetates, on average one additional egg per plant was oviposited on sides scented with the (Z)-3-isomer.
source: Finally, when we compared the two different hexenyl acetates, on average one additional egg per plant was oviposited on sides scented with the (Z)-3-isomer ((Z)-3-hexenyl acetate 1.8 ± 0.3, (E)-2-hexenyl acetate 0.9 ± 0.1; Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by field oviposition assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: OS-specific changes in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio were detectable during one of the two nights in field experiments.
source: As OS-specific changes in the (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratio were detectable during one of the two nights in field experiments, this volatile signal may be encountered by ovipositing Manduca females searching for host plants
evidence: This is a summary of the field volatile collection results.

claim: M. sexta females detect (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate with distinct OSN populations leading to discrete activation patterns in the AL.
source: Functional imaging experiments revealed that M. sexta females detect (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate with distinct OSN populations leading to discrete activation patterns in the AL
evidence: This is a summary of the functional imaging results.

claim: In field experiments Manduca females laid fewer eggs on plants scented with GLV mixtures with increased proportions of (E)-2-GLVs.
source: In field experiments Manduca females laid fewer eggs on plants scented with GLV mixtures with increased proportions of (E)-2-GLVs
evidence: This is a summary of the field oviposition assay results.

claim: Light plays a role for the magnitude of the OS-induced change in the GLV signal.
source: Our initial laboratory studies indicated that OS-induced changes in the GLV-profile of Datura wrightii plants are detectable during day and night, but they also revealed that light plays a role for the magnitude of this change in the signal
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the laboratory volatile collection experiments under different light conditions.

claim: Darkening can cause a temporary burst of GLVs in plants.
source: It has been shown that darkening can cause a temporary burst of GLVs in plants (Graus et al., 2004; Brilli et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Nicotiana attenuata the lipoxygenase NaLOX2, which specifically provides oxygenated fatty acids for the GLV-pathway, has its highest transcript levels during the night.
source: Furthermore, in Nicotiana attenuata the lipoxygenase NaLOX2, which specifically provides oxygenated fatty acids for the GLV-pathway, has its highest transcript levels during the night (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase activity has been found in crude extracts of some plants (alfalfa and soybean).
source: (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase activity has been found in crude extracts of some plants (alfalfa and soybean; Takamura and Gardner, 1996; Noordermeer et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase activity has not been found in N. attenuata.
source: (3Z):(2E)-enal isomerase activity has been found in crude extracts of some plants (alfalfa and soybean; Takamura and Gardner, 1996; Noordermeer et al., 1999), but not in N. attenuata (Allmann and Baldwin, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Circadian rhythm is known to affect volatile emission.
source: Circadian rhythm is also known to affect volatile emission (Goodspeed et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In cotton, acyclic terpenes like β-farnesene and β-ocimene were emitted in a diurnal fashion, while GLVs and few terpenes did not show such a clear diurnal pattern.
source: In cotton, acyclic terpenes like β-farnesene and β-ocimene were emitted in a diurnal fashion, while GLVs and few terpenes did not show such a clear diurnal pattern (Loughrin et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Diurnal-rhythm-dependent emission has been observed in N. tabacum after feeding by larvae of Heliothis virescens, M. sexta and Helicoverpa zea, as these plants released larger amounts of (E)-2-hexenal during the night and emitted other GLVs exclusively in the dark period.
source: Diurnal-rhythm-dependent emission has also been observed in N. tabacum after feeding by larvae of Heliothis virescens, M. sexta and Helicoverpa zea, as these plants released larger amounts of (E)-2-hexenal during the night and emitted other GLVs exclusively in the dark period (De Moraes et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Experiments with lima beans revealed that leaves damaged during the scotophase responded with an almost immediate nocturnal emission of (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, while the main emission of β-ocimene was delayed and peaked during the photophase.
source: Experiments with lima beans revealed that leaves damaged during the scotophase responded with an almost immediate nocturnal emission of (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, while the main emission of β-ocimene was delayed and peaked during the photophase (Arimura et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: GLVs are released instantly from plant tissue upon damage, independent of the time of day.
source: Furthermore, GLVs are released instantly from plant tissue upon damage, independent of the time of day (Turlings et al., 1995; D'Auria et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Terpenoids are released with a delay.
source: Furthermore, GLVs are released instantly from plant tissue upon damage, independent of the time of day (Turlings et al., 1995; D'Auria et al., 2007), while terpenoids are released with a delay (Kant et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Several terpenoids are not released at all during the night as they are linked to photosynthesis.
source: Furthermore, GLVs are released instantly from plant tissue upon damage, independent of the time of day (Turlings et al., 1995; D'Auria et al., 2007), while terpenoids are released with a delay (Kant et al., 2004) and several terpenoids not at all during the night as they are linked to photosynthesis (Arimura et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The insect's olfactory system is highly sophisticated and enables detection of odors at very low concentrations.
source: The insect's olfactory system is highly sophisticated and enables detection of odors at very low concentrations (Hansson et al., 1999; Tanaka et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: OSNs can be tuned to highly specific or to ubiquitous host plant compounds.
source: Plant volatiles are detected by OSNs and these can be tuned to highly specific (Bruce and Pickett, 2011) or to ubiquitous host plant compounds (Hansson et al., 1999; Bruce et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The difference in activation intensity between (E)-2-GLVs and (Z)-3-GLVs is likely a result from different binding affinities of the structural isomers to the olfactory receptor expressed by OSNs targeting the activated glomerulus.
source: This difference in activation intensity is likely a result from different binding affinities of the structural isomers to the olfactory receptor expressed by OSNs targeting the activated glomerulus (Hallem et al., 2004; Hooper et al., 2009)
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the observed differences, supported by citations to previous research on receptor binding.

claim: The investment in isomer-specific receptors and consequently glomeruli to detect and process ubiquitous GLV compounds such as (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate indicates the importance of the information content transferred by these compounds and their respective ratios.
source: Given that all other tested GLVs activated only ROI 2, the investment in isomer-specific receptors and consequently glomeruli to detect and process ubiquitous GLV compounds such as (Z)-3- and (E)-2-hexenyl acetate indicates the importance of the information content transferred by these compounds and their respective ratios
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary significance of the observed neural architecture.

claim: Specific responses to different types of green leaf volatiles have been reported both at physiological and behavioral levels.
source: Specific responses to different types of green leaf volatiles have been reported both at physiological (Hansson et al., 1999; Røstelien et al., 2005) and behavioral levels (Reinecke et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For hexenyl acetate, AL activation patterns elicited by stimulations with mixtures of both structural isomers were purely additive suggesting no mixture interaction at the OSN and AL input levels.
source: For hexenyl acetate, AL activation patterns elicited by stimulations with mixtures of both structural isomers were purely additive suggesting no mixture interaction at the OSN and AL input levels, which is consistent with other studies (Deisig et al., 2006; Carlsson et al., 2007; Silbering and Galizia, 2007; Kuebler et al., 2012)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data, supported by citations to previous research showing similar patterns.

claim: (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate is a rather ubiquitously occurring plant volatile, which is released in large amounts after damage irrespective of its origin.
source: (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate is a rather ubiquitously occurring plant volatile, which is released in large amounts after damage irrespective of its origin (Arimura et al., 2008; Mumm and Dicke, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Electrophysiological experiments revealed that (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate elicited many responses in OSNs on the female M. sexta antenna: 60% of the tested sensilla as well as 21 of 34 cells in the female AL responded to this compound.
source: Electrophysiological experiments revealed that this compound elicited many responses in OSNs on the female M. sexta antenna: 60% of the tested sensilla (Spaethe et al., 2013) as well as 21 of 34 cells in the female AL (Kuebler et al., 2011) responded to this compound
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: (E)-2-hexenyl acetate has rarely been reported in insect-plant interactions.
source: (E)-2-hexenyl acetate, in contrast, has rarely been reported in insect-plant interactions (Whitman and Eller, 1990; Quiroz and Niemeyer, 1998; Williams et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ratio of plant volatiles is an important component of the olfactory signal.
source: Numerous studies suggest that the ratio of plant volatiles is an important component of the olfactory signal (Visser and Avé, 1978; Bruce et al., 2009; Cha et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visser and Avé (1978) found several GLVs playing important roles in host recognition of Leptinotarsa decemlineata.
source: Visser and Avé (1978) found several GLVs playing important roles in host recognition of Leptinotarsa decemlineata
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Augmenting the volatile emission of a potato host plant with the single GLV components (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenol, (E)-2-hexanal or 1-hexanol resulted in a disruption of the orientation of L. decemlineata to the potato plant.
source: Augmenting the volatile emission of a potato host plant with the single GLV components (Z)-3- or (E)-2-hexenol, (E)-2-hexanal or 1-hexanol resulted in a disruption of the orientation of L. decemlineata to the potato plant
evidence: This claim describes results from previous research by Visser and Avé (1978).

claim: Neurons specifically responding to GLVs were found both at the periphery and in the AL of L. decemlineata.
source: Further studies found neurons specifically responding to these GLVs both at the periphery and in the AL of L. decemlineata (De Jong and Visser, 1988a, 1988b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the case of the oriental fruit moth, Grapholita molesta, the ratio of a minor compound to the remaining components of a plant-derived synthetic mixture determined behavioral acceptance of this mixture, which could be associated with the response of two glomeruli in the female AL.
source: In the case of the oriental fruit moth, Grapholita molesta, the ratio of a minor compound to the remaining components of a plant-derived synthetic mixture determined behavioral acceptance of this mixture, which could be associated with the response of two glomeruli in the female AL (Piñero et al., 2008; Najar-Rodriguez et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ovipositing Manduca moths distinguished between different (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios and used these volatile cues to choose oviposition sites associated with less feeding competition and predation.
source: We found that ovipositing Manduca moths distinguished between different (Z)-3/(E)-2-ratios and that they used these volatile cues to choose oviposition sites associated with less feeding competition and predation
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the field oviposition experiments.

claim: Independent of whether the mixtures tested were rather complex in their composition or less complex or consisted of only a single compound, ovipositing Manduca moths continuously made a choice and always preferred the side of the plant that smelled more of (Z)-3-GLVs, or less of (E)-2-GLVs.
source: However, independent of whether the mixtures tested were rather complex in their composition (9:1 vs 1:1 ratios), or less complex (only (Z)-3-GLVs vs only (E)-2-GLVs), or consisted of only a single compound ((Z)-3-hexenyl acetate vs (E)-2-hexenyl acetate) ovipositing Manduca moths continuously made a choice and always preferred the side of the plant that smelled more of (Z)-3-GLVs, or less of (E)-2-GLVs (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is a summary of the field oviposition assay results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: M. sexta moths learn to feed from flowers of non-hosts due to olfactory conditioning.
source: It has been shown that M. sexta moths learn to feed from flowers of non-hosts due to olfactory conditioning (Riffell et al., 2008, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Experience can shape female oviposition choice as it has been shown in other moth species.
source: Experience could as well shape female oviposition choice as it has been shown in other moth species (Rietdorf and Steidle, 2002; Olsson et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The retention of odor memory learned at the larval stage onto the adult stage has been shown to occur in M. sexta.
source: The retention of odor memory learned at the larval stage onto the adult stage has been shown to occur in M. sexta (Blackiston et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The AL, the first odor processing center of the insect brain, has the capacity to resolve the composition of GLV blends as emitted by highly relevant host plants.
source: Our results show that the AL, the first odor processing center of the insect brain, has the capacity to resolve the composition of GLV blends as emitted by highly relevant host plants
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional imaging results.

claim: Gravid females make an informed choice and prefer oviposition sites with reduced predation and competition risks for their offspring, as indicated by the plant volatile bouquet.
source: Correspondingly, gravid females make an informed choice. They prefer oviposition sites with reduced predation and competition risks for their offspring, as indicated by the plant volatile bouquet
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of the study.
